summary: Redwood Optimize walkthrough focusing on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations for Silverpine's real-time summarization product. Discussed tradeoffs between latency and cost, prefetching strategies, optimal batch-concurrency sweet spots, and a tailored cost projection. Agreed next steps: Silverpine will send traffic traces, Redwood will deliver a cost model spreadsheet and schedule a PoC kickoff.
topics: Prefix cache vs KV cache tradeoffs
Dedicated vs hosted routing for latency SLOs
transcript:
[00:00] Rachel (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We have about 50 minutes. Quick intros?
[00:08] Priya (Silverpine): Priya here, head of ML at Silverpine, we own the summarization pipeline. Jules, Tom and Aisha are with me.
[00:15] Jules: Jules — infra. We run a mix of on-prem GPUs and cloud bursts, lots of short requests, typical token lengths around 80 to 220.
[00:22] Diego (SE): Great, Diego from Redwood — I'll drive the Optimize portion, focus on batching, prefix & K-V cache strategies. Apologies if I mangle some names, my connection is a bit spotty.
[00:32] Tom (CTO): Quick note — latency 95th needs to be under 350ms for the interactive flows, and cost is a big factor.
[00:40] Rachel: Cool. Goal today: show practical recs and a cost model you can use to pick config. We'll call out dedicated/private considerations when it matters.
[00:50] Diego: Alright, starting with a high-level. Two levers we work with in Optimize: batching/concurrency and caching. Batching reduces per-token compute by amortizing kernel overhead, but increases queueing latency. Caches reduce repeated prefix compute — prefix cache (on-request prefix reuse) and KV cache (per-token state reuse across requests).
[01:10] Priya: Could you define KV cache in your terms? We've seen different uses.
[01:15] Diego: Sure. In our docs we call it "KV cache" meaning the key/value attention caches that are appended for autoregressive decoding — so between requests if you can reuse the cache (e.g., same conversation or same prompt prefix) that saves recomputing cross-attention for those tokens. People also call it state caching, K-V cask sometimes in transcribe — sorry, typo there.
[01:34] Aisha: How much savings are we talking? Our workload has a high variance in prefix reuse — some users send the same company boilerplate, some unique text.
[01:43] Diego: It depends. Rough ballpark: if you have 40% prefix reuse, you could see 20-35% token-cost reduction relative to no cache, more if the reused prefix is long. The spreadsheet I'll send models by prefix-length distribution — short prefixes (10-30 tokens) give smaller gains than 100+ token repeated boilerplates.
[02:00] Rachel: We're going to walk through a sample Silverpine run: avg input 120 tokens, response 80 tokens, spike concurrency 40 qps for interactive.
[02:12] Jules: Our current infra has an average tail 95 latency ~410ms, so we need to shave that.
[02:18] Diego: Two immediate knobs: reduce queuing by lowering batch-max-wait or reduce batch size target by tuning concurrency, and enable prefix caching where applicable. But there's a cost tradeoff: smaller batches = higher cost per token typically.
[02:34] [03:02] Diego: Let me pull up the Optimize console (link shared: https://app.redwood.ai/optimize/silverpine-playbook). Note: link in recording, deck also available: https://drive.redwood.ai/silverpine-optimize-deck.pdf
[03:12] Priya: I saw that in the invite, thanks.
[03:16] Diego: On the console I have a simulated cost model. For baseline (no cache, batch target 16, concurrency 8) we estimate $0.024 per 1k tokens. If you switch to batch target 32 and concurrency 16 you drop to $0.018 per 1k, but 95th latency increases by ~40-60ms in our sim for this traffic shape.
[03:36] Tom: Those numbers are per hosted price? How does dedicated change it?
[03:40] Diego: Hosted uses per-token unit pricing; Dedicated is effectively reserved GPU resources, so per-token marginal can be lower but you pay reserved capacity. In the spreadsheet we'll show amortized cost per token at different utilization levels. Dedicated becomes attractive if you have steady utilization above ~60-70% of capacity.
[03:56] Jules: For our workloads we have heavy diurnal spikes and a baseline steady traffic. Could we use mixed routing?
[04:02] Diego: Yes, smart routing is a built-in pattern: route steady low-latency traffic to Dedicated, and burst to Hosted or other regions. Also you can set fallbacks. We'll show a hybrid config later.
[04:12] [05:00] Diego: Now caching specifics. Two modes we suggest: prefix cache at the request level — store computed activations for common prompt prefixes (fast and simple), and KV cache which is more powerful for streaming or multi-turn reuse. Prefix cache is smaller surface area, easier to evict; KV cache depends on whether you can persist state tied to a conversation id.
[05:20] Priya: We don't persist conversation across sessions. Most of our reuse is within the single request (boilerplate instructions). Prefix cache sounds like it might help.
[05:30] Diego: Exactly. For single-request boilerplate, prefix cache reduces the repeated prefix decode. In our simulations, enabling prefix cache for 35% of requests reduced per-token compute by ~16% and 95th latency by ~30ms because fewer tokens get re-processed.
[05:48] Aisha: Any caveats with correctness? We worry about tokenization differences and prompt normalization.
[05:55] Diego: Good point. Prefix cache requires canonicalization: trim whitespace, normalize punctuation, maybe hash normal forms. Our Optimize product includes a canonicalizer you can configure; we have a threshold for prefix-match similarity (exact or fuzzy). There's a small risk of false-positive cache hits if you normalize too aggressively — you might serve slightly different outputs. We recommend logging sample hits and running a small A/B test initially.
[06:16] [07:10] Diego: Now on prefetching: if you can detect predictable next prompts (e.g., follow-up templates), you can precompute the prefix activations and keep them warm. This helps hide kernel latency at the expense of compute and memory. For Silverpine's flow, if 20% of users follow the same follow-up path, prefetching those prefixes would shave 60-80ms off the median for those flows but cost extra GPU cycles for the prefetch.
[07:40] Priya: Interesting. How does prefetch interact with batching? Do prefetch ops get batched?
[07:46] Diego: Yes, prefetch requests are batched like normal requests but can be scheduled on lower-priority lanes. You can treat them as background work. We expose lane priority and you can throttle prefetching to keep SLOs intact.
[07:58] [09:00] Diego: Let's walk a concrete cost example from the sim. Baseline: 1M requests per month, avg 200 tokens total per req = 200M tokens. At $0.024/1k = $4,800. With prefix cache hitting 35% and average saved tokens 60 each, net tokens saved = 1M * .35 * 60 = 21M tokens => $504 saved direct (plus latency gains). With batch tuning to reduce per-token cost to $0.018, you get base cost $3,600; with prefix caching on top you end up at approx $3,200. So combined wins are meaningful.
[09:34] Tom: That delta looks promising. Do these numbers include KV cache memory overhead?
[09:37] Diego: The per-token price is compute-only in the hosted model; KV cache increases memory usage (RAM/GPU memory) and may slightly reduce throughput per GPU, so there's a throughput vs memory trade. In dedicated we size machines to accommodate KV cache. Our sizing guide suggests adding ~0.5-1GB of GPU memory per active cache slot depending on model and sequence length.
[09:58] [10:30] Jules: What about quantization — can we combine 4-bit quant with KV cache?
[10:35] Diego: Yes, quantization works fine. The runtime stores activations in float32 for cache, but model weights can be quantized. There are some micro differences in perf; our Optimize suggestions include quantization profiles per-model that balance quality vs throughput.
[10:52] Priya: Can we see a simulated throughput curve? Like latency vs qps under different batch targets.
[10:58] Diego: Yup — I pulled a few charts. (Diego shares screen) For your token distribution, batch_target 8 + concurrency 12 gives median 120ms and 95th 320ms at 40qps; moving to batch_target 32 pushes 95th to ~390ms at same qps. So pick batch_target around 12-16 to hit your 350ms 95th SLO.
[11:25] Aisha: Could we adopt dynamic batch sizing? Increase target in off-peak?
[11:30] Diego: Absolutely. We support adaptive batching policies: scale batch_target by observed queue depth and latency tail. You can also pin a max_latency SLO and let the controller shrink batches when tail breaches.
[11:42] [12:20] Diego: Now a short note on instrumentation — Redwood Console exposes per-route token breakdown (prompt vs completion), cache hit rates, and latency percentiles. We recommend instrumenting the key routes and a small set of prompt templates to monitor regressions post-rollout.
[12:38] Priya: We have strict audit requirements — can Optimize produce logs that are redteam/forensics friendly?
[12:44] Lina (Product): Yes, you can stream event logs to your SIEM, and we support audit-level sampling for caching decisions. Also SSO/SAML and SCIM for RBAC.
[12:54] Tom: On security — if we use prefix cache on hosted, are prefixes stored encrypted?
[12:58] Rachel: Hosted stores cache contents encrypted at rest; we also offer a Private deployment where you can control encryption keys via KMS/HSM if needed. Data residency controls via region pinning.
[13:10] [14:00] Priya: Back to performance — what about multi-model routing? We sometimes fall back to a smaller cheaper model for low-priority requests.
[14:06] Diego: Smart routing can detect low-priority class and route to a cheaper model. You can also set fallbacks when a target model is at capacity. Optimize can simulate the blended cost. For example, routing 25% of low-importance requests to a cheaper model saved an additional ~12% on monthly spend in our example.
[14:28] Jules: For the PoC we're thinking to run ~48 hours of live traffic replay through your bench. What do you need?
[14:34] Diego: Prefer raw request logs (anonymized), a token-length histogram, and a few representative templates. We'll provide a harness (gRPC) and a load script. We'll also ask you to whitelist Redwood's test IPs for any Private setups.
[14:48] Priya: We'll need an NDA in place for the logs.
[14:50] Rachel: We can share standard NDA; our legal can ping yours after this call.
[14:56] [15:40] Diego: Quick caveat on measurements: we simulate tail latency using a queuing model — it's close but real-world tails sometimes diverge due to network jitter and kernel scheduling. That's why we always recommend a short PoC to validate.
[16:02] Tom: Understood. Any surprises we should watch for?
[16:06] Diego: Cold-cache misses on KV can be painful if your hit rate is lower than expected. Also, overly aggressive canonicalization can change outputs. And prefetching can increase baseline utilization, so be mindful of capacity headroom.
[16:28] [17:00] Priya: About canonicalization — can we tune similarity thresholds per template?
[17:04] Diego: Yes, Optimize lets you set per-template normalization and match thresholds; you can also view example false hits and exclude templates from caching.
[17:18] Aisha: Let's talk rollout strategy — can we do gradual enablement?
[17:22] Rachel: We recommend a canary: 5% traffic with caching on, monitor quality/regressions for 48 hours, then ramp 25/50/100% as metrics look good. We'll automate rollout via the Console.
[17:36] [18:30] Diego: Alright, recap of concrete recommendations for Silverpine: 1) Start with prefix cache for templates and canonicalization rules; 2) set batch_target ~12-16 for your 40qps shape to meet 95th 350ms; 3) run PoC with live replay for 48-72 hours to validate; 4) simulate hybrid routing for bursts and consider dedicated for steady baseline if utilization >60%.
[18:56] Priya: That feels actionable. Can you send the cost model CSV with scenarios?
[19:00] Rachel: Yes — action item. We'll send three scenarios: baseline, prefix cache enabled, prefix cache + batch tuning.
[19:06] Tom: Also, include a dedicated sizing sheet so we can evaluate reserved cost.
[19:10] Diego: We'll include reserved amortization curves.
[19:14] [20:00] Priya: One last Q on SLA — what is Redwood's SLO/penalty for Dedicated?
[20:06] Rachel: Dedicated comes with an SLA and uptime guarantee; specifics depend on the contract tier, but typical are >99.9% uptime and latency targets in the appendix. We'll have sales follow up.
[20:18] Jules: Good, next steps and owners?
[20:22] Rachel: I'll summarize. (Rachel lists next steps) 
[20:34] [21:00] Diego: Anything else from Silverpine?
[21:06] Priya: Nope, looks good. We'll start prepping logs.
[21:12] Tom: Add our security contact to the thread.
[21:15] Rachel: Will do. Thanks everyone. Ending call.
[21:22] [END] Note: Transcript automated by Fireflies. Occasional mis-hearings likely (e.g., K-V cask/kv cache typos), please refer to shared deck and cost spreadsheet for canonical numbers.
